title: Women on the Mat
bigQuestion: Why did women wait so long for their own places on the mat, and who opened the doors?

story.title: A New Sheet on the Wall
story.kicker: A coach pins up a list of weight classes, and some names appear for the first time.
paragraphs: It is the fall of 2021 in an Illinois high school. A wrestling coach walks into the practice room with a sheet of paper. He pins it to the cork board beside the door. The old sheet on that board listed only boys. The new sheet is headed with two words: girls wrestling.

The Illinois High School Association, or IHSA, was founded in 1900. It crowned its first boys wrestling state champions in 1937. For more than eighty years after that, there was no girls state series. Girls who wanted to wrestle joined boys' teams and faced boys in matches.

Now the IHSA had approved a separate state series for girls. The first girls state finals would come in 2022, at the end of the 2021–22 season. The sheet on the cork board lists weight classes, each with blank lines for names. Several girls already on the team write their names on it.

The sheet is small, but it stands for a long story. That story runs through ancient Greece, a Tokyo judo hall, a federal law signed in 1972, court cases, and the Olympic Games. At each step, someone had to decide who may stand on the mat.
story.think: Why might a separate weight-class sheet for girls matter to a wrestler who had already been on a boys' team?

lessons.title: Sparta, Olympia and Kyniska
lessons.mainIdea: Ancient Greek sources show some girls exercising and wrestling in Sparta, while the Olympic Games at Olympia shut most women out.
reading: The Greek writer Plutarch lived about 46 to 119 CE. In his *Life of Lycurgus*, he describes the laws of old Sparta. He says Spartan girls exercised in running, wrestling, and throwing the discus and javelin. Plutarch wrote centuries after these laws, so historians read his account with care.

Most Greek cities kept girls at home. The Olympic Games at Olympia were for men only. The travel writer Pausanias, in the 100s CE, wrote that married women were not allowed even to watch. He also tells a *legend* about a mother who sneaked in to watch her son. Historians treat that tale as a story, not a record.

One woman did win at Olympia. Kyniska was a Spartan princess. Her four-horse chariot team won in 396 and 392 BCE. Owners, not drivers, were named as winners, so she won without entering the track. A stone base with her victory inscription survives. Pausanias also wrote of the Heraia, separate footraces for unmarried girls at Olympia.

words.d: a biography by the Greek writer Plutarch that describes the laws of ancient Sparta
a traditional story told as history that cannot be proven with records
ancient footraces for unmarried girls held at Olympia, described by Pausanias

look.title: Two Writers, Two Kinds of Evidence

choices: They exercised in running, wrestling and throwing
They competed at the men's Olympic Games
They were banned from all exercise

check.why: In the Life of Lycurgus, Plutarch says Spartan girls ran, wrestled, and threw the discus and javelin.

check.q: How did Kyniska win at Olympia?
choices: She wrestled in the men's event
She sneaked in to watch her son
She owned the winning four-horse chariot team
check.why: Chariot owners were named as winners, so Kyniska won as owner in 396 and 392 BCE.

check.q: Why do historians read Plutarch's account of Sparta with care?
choices: He wrote only about the Olympic Games
He wrote centuries after the laws he describes
check.why: Plutarch lived about 46 to 119 CE, long after the early Spartan laws, so his account is not an eyewitness record.

lessons.title: Sumo's Ring and Women
lessons.mainIdea: Professional sumo in Japan still keeps women out of its ring, while amateur sumo holds women's events.
reading: Sumo is Japan's oldest recorded form of wrestling. The ring is called the *dohyo*. It is a raised clay platform with a circle made of straw bales. Professional sumo is run by the Japan Sumo Association. It traces its modern form to 1925.

Women took part in sumo in the past. By the 1700s, women's sumo shows, called *onna-zumo*, were staged in Edo Japan as entertainment. Officials restricted these shows at times. Professional sumo, though, kept its dohyo for men. The association says the rule follows its customs, which are tied to Shinto rites.

The rule has drawn public protest. In 2000, Fusae Ohta, the governor of Osaka, asked to hand a prize to a winner in the ring. The association refused. In April 2018, in Maizuru, a mayor collapsed while speaking in the ring. Women gave him first aid and were told by announcement to leave. The association's chairman later apologized for that announcement.

Amateur sumo is different. The International Sumo Federation was founded in 1992. It runs world championships with divisions for women as well as men. So two sumo bodies answer the question of who may stand in the ring in two different ways.

words.d: the raised clay ring used in sumo, marked by a circle of straw bales
women's sumo shows staged in Japan by the 1700s
the body that runs professional sumo in Japan

choices: It holds women's divisions in amateur championships

check.why: The amateur federation, founded in 1992, holds women's divisions; professional sumo keeps its ring for men.

lessons.title: The Kodokan's Women's Section
lessons.mainIdea: Kanō Jigorō taught some women judo, and the Kodokan opened a formal women's section in 1926.
reading: Kanō Jigorō founded the *Kodokan* in Tokyo in 1882. The Kodokan is the home school of judo. At first, nearly all its students were men and boys. Kanō also worked as a teacher and school leader. He believed physical education belonged in schools.

Kanō taught some women judo privately by the 1890s. For women, the Kodokan set up separate classes and ways of practice. In 1926, it opened a formal *women's section*. Women trained in their own room with their own teachers.

Separate training came with limits. For decades, women at the Kodokan did not enter contests the way men did. Their ranks also stopped lower than men's ranks. Keiko Fukuda began training at the Kodokan in 1935. She would spend the next seventy years pushing against those limits.

words.d: the judo school Kanō Jigorō founded in Tokyo in 1882; the home institute of judo
the separate division for women at the Kodokan, opened formally in 1926

check.why: Women trained separately, and for decades their ranks stopped below the ranks men could reach.

lessons.title: One Sentence in 1972
lessons.mainIdea: Title IX, signed in 1972, bans sex discrimination in any school program that gets federal money, including sports.
reading: On June 23, 1972, President Richard Nixon signed the Education Amendments of 1972. One part is called *Title IX*. Its main rule is a single sentence of 37 words. The sentence never mentions sports.

The law covers any education program that receives *federal financial assistance*. That means money from the national government. Almost every public school and college gets such money. So Title IX reached school teams, including wrestling rooms and gyms.

Members of Congress pushed the law forward. Edith Green of Oregon and Patsy Mink of Hawaii led in the House. Birch Bayh of Indiana led in the Senate. Mink died in 2002. That year, Congress renamed the law the Patsy T. Mink Equal Opportunity in Education Act.

Rules for sports came later. Federal rules written in 1975 explained how schools should give girls a fair chance to play. Schools were given several years to comply. The Education Department's Office for Civil Rights handles complaints when students believe a school is breaking the law.

words.d: part of the Education Amendments of 1972 that bans sex discrimination in federally funded education programs
money from the U.S. national government given to schools and programs
treating people unfairly because of who they are, such as their sex or race

look.title: The Words of Title IX
look.text: No person in the United States shall, on the basis of sex, be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any education program or activity receiving Federal financial assistance.
look.cite: Title IX, Education Amendments of 1972, 20 U.S.C. section 1681(a)
look.prompt: The sentence never says the word sports. Which words in it made school teams part of the law?

check.q: Which president signed Title IX in 1972?
check.why: President Richard Nixon signed the Education Amendments of 1972 on June 23, 1972.

check.q: Why did Title IX reach school sports even though it never says sports?
choices: It covers any education program that receives federal money
It was written by the IHSA
It was a rule of the Olympic Games
check.why: School teams are education programs, and nearly all public schools receive federal financial assistance.

check.q: In 2002, Title IX was renamed for which member of Congress?
check.why: After Patsy Mink of Hawaii died in 2002, Congress renamed the law in her honor.

lessons.title: Why Combat Sports Moved Slowly
lessons.mainIdea: Title IX brought many more girls into school sports, but girls' wrestling teams grew slowly, one state at a time.
reading: Title IX changed who played school sports. The National Federation of State High School Associations counted about 295,000 girls in high school sports in 1971–72. By the 2010s, the count was more than three million. Basketball, track, volleyball and soccer grew fastest.

Wrestling grew more slowly for girls. Schools could meet the law by adding other sports. Many schools had one wrestling room and one team, and it was a boys' team. Each state *association*, the group that runs school sports, decided whether to hold a separate girls' tournament.

For years, girls who wanted to wrestle joined boys' teams. In the late 1990s, a few states began separate girls' state tournaments. Hawaii and Texas were among the first. Other states followed across the 2000s and 2010s. Illinois joined in the 2021–22 season.

Colleges moved slowly too. In 2020, the NCAA named women's wrestling an *emerging sport*. That label is a step toward a full national championship. Before the NCAA acted, a national women's college championship was run by other groups, and many teams competed as clubs.

words.d: a group that runs school sports in a state, such as the IHSA in Illinois
an NCAA label for a women's sport that is growing toward a national championship

check.why: Many schools had only a boys' team, so girls who wanted to wrestle joined it.

lessons.title: Boxing Goes to Court
lessons.mainIdea: A 1993 court case opened U.S. amateur boxing to women, and women's world amateur championships began in 2001.
reading: Women boxed in the United States long before rules allowed it in amateur contests. Some women's bouts were staged as shows in the 1800s and 1900s. But *USA Boxing*, the body that runs amateur boxing in the country, banned women from its events.

In 1993, a sixteen-year-old named Dallas Malloy went to court in Washington State. She challenged USA Boxing's ban. A judge ruled in her favor. That October she boxed in the first women's bout *sanctioned* by USA Boxing. Sanctioned means approved and run under the body's rules.
Other bodies followed. The world amateur boxing body held its first women's world championships in 2001, in Scranton, Pennsylvania. Eleven years later, women's boxing would reach the Olympic Games.

words.d: the governing body for amateur boxing in the United States
approved and run under the rules of a governing body

look.title: A Ban and a Ruling
look.text: Before 1993, a teenage girl who trained in a boxing gym could hit bags, spar and work with a coach. But she could not enter an amateur contest run by USA Boxing. After a judge ruled for Dallas Malloy, the same gym could send her to a sanctioned bout.
look.prompt: What changed for the girl after 1993: her gym, her training, or the rules of the governing body?

check.why: Sixteen-year-old Dallas Malloy went to court and won, then boxed in the first sanctioned women's bout.

check.why: A sanctioned bout is approved and run under the rules of a body such as USA Boxing.

check.q: When were the first women's world amateur boxing championships held?
check.why: The first women's world amateur championships were held in 2001 in Scranton, Pennsylvania.

lessons.title: Rusty Kanokogi's Medal
lessons.mainIdea: Rusty Kanokogi lost a judo medal in 1959 for being a woman and later organized the first women's world judo championships in 1980.
reading: Rena "Rusty" Glickman grew up in Brooklyn, New York, in the 1930s and 1940s. She began judo as a young woman, at a time when very few American women trained in it. Later she married a Japanese judo teacher and took the name Kanokogi.

In 1959, she entered a YMCA judo tournament in Utica, New York, on a team with men. Her team won. Then officials asked whether she was a woman. When she said yes, they took her *medal* away. At that time, the tournament had no place for women.

Kanokogi spent the next decades building one. She raised money for a women's world championship, including by mortgaging her own house. The first *Women's World Judo Championships* were held in New York City in 1980. In 1988, she coached the U.S. women's team when women's judo was shown at the Seoul Olympics.

In 2009, the New York State YMCA gave her a gold medal for the 1959 tournament. It came fifty years late, but it put the 1959 result on the record. She died in November of that year, at age 74, in New York.

words.d: a metal award given to a winner at a tournament
the first world judo title event for women, held in New York City in 1980

choices: She was not from New York

check.why: Fifty years after the tournament, the New York State YMCA awarded her a gold medal.

lessons.title: Keiko Fukuda's Long Climb
lessons.mainIdea: Keiko Fukuda trained in judo for more than seventy years and became the first woman to hold judo's tenth degree.
reading: Keiko Fukuda was born in Tokyo in 1913. Her grandfather, Fukuda Hachinosuke, had taught jujutsu to the young Kanō Jigorō. In 1935, she began training in the Kodokan's women's section.

Judo marks skill with *dan* ranks, or degrees, from first up to tenth. For decades, the Kodokan held women below the ranks men could reach. In 1972, Fukuda became one of the first women the Kodokan promoted to sixth degree.

Fukuda moved to the United States in the 1960s and taught women in the San Francisco Bay Area. In 2006, the Kodokan made her ninth degree. In 2011, USA Judo awarded her tenth degree, the highest rank. She was the first woman to hold it. She died in 2013, at age 99.

words.d: a degree of rank in judo and many other arts, counted from first to tenth
the national governing body for judo in the United States

lessons.title: Olympic Doors, Sport by Sport
lessons.mainIdea: Women entered Olympic combat sports one at a time, from fencing in 1924 to boxing in 2012.
reading: The modern Olympic Games began in Athens in 1896. Men's wrestling and fencing were on that first program. Women first competed at the Olympics in 1900, in sports such as tennis and golf. Combat sports opened to women much later.

Fencing came first. Women's foil fencing joined the Paris Games in 1924. Judo was a men's event from the Tokyo Games of 1964. Women's judo was a *demonstration event* at Seoul in 1988, which means medals did not count. It became a full medal event at Barcelona in 1992.

Taekwondo became a medal sport at Sydney in 2000 for men and women together. Women's freestyle wrestling was added at Athens in 2004. Japan's Kaori Icho won gold in her class at every Games from 2004 through 2016. Boxing came last, at London in 2012.

words.d: a sport shown at the Olympic Games in which medals do not count
the official list of sports and events at an Olympic Games

lessons.title: Equal Sheets in Judo and Taekwondo
lessons.mainIdea: Olympic judo and taekwondo now give women the same number of weight classes as men.
reading: A *weight class* groups athletes of similar body weight. Each class has its own gold, silver and bronze medals. So the number of classes decides how many women can win Olympic titles.

Judo gave women seven classes from 1992, the same number as men. The current women's limits are 48, 52, 57, 63, 70 and 78 kilograms, plus a class over 78. At Tokyo in 2021, judo added a *mixed team* event with men and women on the same team.

Taekwondo was equal from its first medal Games in 2000. Men and women each have four classes. The women's classes are up to 49, 57 and 67 kilograms, plus a class over 67. The sport's world body, World Taekwondo, keeps the same count for both.

words.d: a group of athletes of similar body weight who compete only against each other
an event in which men and women compete on the same team

lessons.title: Growing Lists in Boxing and Wrestling
lessons.mainIdea: Women's Olympic boxing and wrestling began with few weight classes and added more over later Games.
reading: When women's wrestling joined the Athens Games in 2004, it had four weight classes. Men had seven freestyle classes that year. In 2016, at Rio de Janeiro, women gained six classes. Now each style of wrestling has six classes for its athletes.

Women's boxing began at London in 2012 with three classes out of thirteen boxing events. Nicola Adams of Great Britain, Katie Taylor of Ireland and Claressa Shields of the United States won the first three golds. Shields, from Flint, Michigan, was seventeen.

Later Games shifted classes from men to women. Tokyo had five women's boxing classes. Paris in 2024 had six women's classes and seven men's. Each change was made by the *International Olympic Committee*, or IOC, with the sport's world body.

words.d: the body that runs the Olympic Games and decides which events are held
a style of Olympic wrestling; women's Olympic wrestling is held in this style

check.why: The IOC runs the Games and sets the events, working with each sport's world body.

lessons.title: Illinois Girls Take the Mat
lessons.mainIdea: The IHSA held its first girls wrestling state finals in 2022, eighty-five years after its first boys champions.
reading: The *IHSA* runs high school sports in Illinois. It was founded in 1900. Its first boys wrestling state champions were crowned in 1937. For decades, the state series had only boys' brackets.

Girls in Illinois wrestled anyway, on boys' teams. Then the IHSA approved a separate girls series. The first girls wrestling *state finals* came in 2022, at the end of the 2021–22 season. That was eighty-five years after the first boys champions.

A separate series changed who could win a title. Before, a girl could reach a state final only by beating boys. After 2022, girls' brackets gave girls their own path to a state medal. Illinois joined a national wave of states that added girls' wrestling.

words.d: the Illinois High School Association, founded in 1900, which runs high school sports in Illinois
the last rounds of a state tournament, where champions are decided
